items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 15): Three students each measure the mass of the same metal sample. Is student 3's result reproducible? Why or why not?

body.html: A result is reproducible if other experimenters, using the same procedure, get results that agree (their uncertainty ranges overlap).
Student 3's range (51.8 to 52.2 g) overlaps student 1's (51.9 to 52.7 g) and student 2's (52.1 to 53.1 g).

answer.html: Yes. The other two students' ranges overlap with student 3's, so student 3's result was reproduced within the uncertainties.

check.html: Student 2's lowest value (52.1 g) is below student 3's highest value (52.2 g), so there is overlap.

items.title: Lesson 3, the beaker question (page 15): Compare the precision of a beaker with divisions every 25 mL to a graduated cylinder with divisions every 2 mL

body.html: Precision of a measurement is one-half of the smallest division.
Cylinder: <sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>(2 mL) = 1 mL. Beaker: <sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>(25 mL) = 12.5 mL. The ratio is 12.5 / 1 = 12.5.

answer.html: The beaker is precise to about ±12.5 mL, which is 12.5 times less precise than the graduated cylinder (±1 mL).

check.html: Smaller divisions give a smaller uncertainty.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 12 "Infer": A kitchen scale reads 0.0 g with nothing on it. When a 200.0 g standard mass is placed on it, the scale reads 207 g. Is this instrument accurate? Why or why not?

body.html: Zero reading: 0.0 g (correct). Standard mass: 200.0 g. Scale reading: 207 g.
Two-point calibration: (1) check that the scale reads zero with nothing on it, (2) check it against an accepted standard.
The scale passes the zero check but fails the second check. The error is

answer.html: No. It reads zero correctly, but it reads about 7 g (3.5%) too high with the standard mass, so it is not accurate and should be recalibrated.

check.html: An instrument can read zero correctly and still be wrong at larger readings.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 16): Two players each throw five darts at a dartboard. Player A's darts land in a tight cluster 10 cm to the left of the bull's-eye. Player B's darts are spread widely, but their average position is at the bull's-eye. Compare and contrast the precision and accuracy of the two players.

body.html: Precision is how tightly repeated results agree (small spread); accuracy is how close results are to the accepted or true value (the bull's-eye).
Player A's darts are close together (high precision) but all off target (low accuracy). Player B's darts are scattered (low precision), but their average is on target (accurate on average).

answer.html: Both describe the quality of the throws. A is precise but not accurate; B is accurate on average but not precise. A player who is both precise and accurate would put all five darts in the bull's-eye.

check.html: Like a bent instrument (precise but wrong) compared with a coarse but correctly zeroed one.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 13 "Identify": A passenger and the driver both read the same needle on a car's speedometer. The driver, looking straight at the dial, reads 90 km/h. The passenger, looking from an angle, reads 96 km/h. How far did parallax shift the passenger's reading?

body.html: Straight-on reading: 90 km/h. Angled reading: 96 km/h.
Parallax is the apparent shift of an object's position when it is viewed from a different angle. The correct reading is taken with your eye directly in front of the mark.

answer.html: The parallax shifted the passenger's reading by 6 km/h (about 6.7% too high). The driver's straight-on reading, 90 km/h, is the correct one.

check.html: The shift is small compared with the reading, as expected for a modest viewing angle.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 12: A digital caliper displays 0.01 mm divisions but reads 0.35 mm when it is closed on nothing. A plastic ruler has 1 mm divisions and is printed correctly. Compare the precision and accuracy of the two instruments.

body.html: Precision is the exactness of the instrument; accuracy is whether it gives the true value.

The caliper's precision (0.01 mm) is much finer than the ruler's (1 mm). But its closed reading should be zero and is 0.35 mm, so every measurement is shifted by 0.35 mm unless that offset is corrected.

answer.html: The caliper is more precise (finer divisions) but, with the uncorrected offset, less accurate; the ruler is less precise but accurate.

check.html: Fine divisions do not guarantee correct readings.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 13: The hook at the end of a tape measure slides back and forth by a distance equal to the hook's thickness. Why is this a good design?

body.html: When you hook the end over the edge of an object (an outside measurement), the hook slides out so the zero mark lines up with the edge. When you push the hook against a surface (an inside measurement), it slides in. In both cases the slide equals the thickness of the hook, so the reading starts at the true zero of the scale.

answer.html: The sliding hook adjusts by exactly its own thickness, so the tape reads correctly whether you pull it against an edge or push it against a wall. This keeps the zero point accurate.

check.html: This is like checking the zero reading in a two-point calibration.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 14: A digital balance reads 0.3 g with nothing on it. Does this error affect the precision or the accuracy of its readings?

answer.html: It affects accuracy. Every reading is 0.3 g too high, so the readings are wrong by a fixed amount. The balance can still show the same finest division as before, so its precision (the smallest division it can show) is unchanged. Pressing the tare button to reset the zero fixes the problem.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 15: A runner's time in a race is reported as 12.8 s. What does this tell you about the time?

body.html: The last digit is uncertain; the precision is half the smallest division, here ±0.05 s.

answer.html: The time is between about 12.75 s and 12.85 s (12.8 ± 0.05 s); that is, it rounds to 12.8 s to the nearest tenth of a second.

check.html: The timer did not claim to know the time to the hundredth of a second.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 17: A swim coach times 8 laps of a 400-m run with a stopwatch that reads to the nearest 0.1 s and reports the average lap time as 41.7625 s. How much confidence do you have in this result?

body.html: Clock precision 0.1 s; 8 laps timed; reported average 41.7625 s per 400-m lap.
A result cannot be more precise than the measurement it comes from.
The total time for 8 laps would be read to 0.1 s:
That total has 4 significant figures. Dividing by the exact count 8 keeps 4 significant figures, so the average should be reported as 41.76 s, not 41.7625 s. The extra digits have no meaning.

answer.html: Limited confidence in the extra digits. Timing 8 laps and averaging is a good technique, but 41.7625 s claims more precision than a 0.1 s stopwatch allows. It should be reported as about 41.76 s (the last digit uncertain), and we would also want to know about reaction-time error at the start and stop.

check.html: An uncertainty of ±0.1 s on 334.1 s is about 0.03% overall, so the result is still good, just over-reported.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 16): Compare and contrast precision and accuracy

answer.html: Both describe the quality of measurements. Precision is the exactness (fine detail or small uncertainty) of a measurement, set by the instrument and technique. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the accepted true value. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (a bent micrometer), or accurate but not precise (a coarse beaker that is correctly zeroed).

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 12: A bent micrometer versus a new meter stick

body.html: Precision is the exactness of the instrument; accuracy is whether it gives the true value.
The micrometer's precision is 0.001 mm (finer than the meter stick, perhaps 1 mm divisions). Because it is bent, readings are wrong.

answer.html: The bent micrometer is more precise (finer divisions) than the meter stick but less accurate (readings are off), while the new high-quality meter stick is less precise but accurate.

check.html: Fine divisions do not guarantee correct readings.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 13: Rulers with 0 set in from the edge

body.html: The end of a ruler gets worn, chipped, or dirty, and it can be hard to line the edge up with an object's edge. If 0 is set in a few millimeters, the zero mark is not affected by wear and can be lined up with the object directly.

answer.html: Wear or damage on the edge would shift every reading, but a zero mark set in from the edge stays correct and lets you line up the start of the object clearly, so measurements are more accurate.

check.html: This is like checking the zero reading in a two-point calibration.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 14: Does parallax affect precision?

answer.html: No. Parallax shifts the reading to the wrong value, so it affects accuracy. Precision (the finest division the instrument can show) is set by the instrument and technique, and is the same however you view it.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 17: Average lap time reported as 65.414 s

body.html: Clock precision 0.1 s; 7 laps timed; reported average 65.414 s for a 2.4-km lap.
A result cannot be more precise than the measurement it comes from.

The total time for 7 laps would be read to 0.1 s, about 65.414 × 7 = 457.9 s (4 significant figures). Dividing by the exact count 7 keeps 4 significant figures, so the average should be reported as 65.41 s, not 65.414 s. The extra digit has no meaning. (The 2.4-km length has only two significant figures as well.)

answer.html: Limited confidence. Timing 7 laps and averaging is a good technique, but the stated 65.414 s claims more precision than a 0.1 s clock allows. It should be reported as about 65.41 s (the last digit uncertain), and we would also want to know about reaction-time error at the start and stop.

check.html: An uncertainty of ±0.1 s on 457.9 s is about 0.02% overall, so the result is still good, just over-reported.
